messages.subject: Unknown groupName using "HuGene-1_0-st-v1_Ensembl47.cdf"
parts:
Hi, all. I used "HuGene-1_0-st-v1_Ensembl47.cdf" to annotate the Human
Gene 1.0 ST Array Cel files. And I failed mapping the groupNames to
the genome.

The whole annotation processes were successful. However, when mapping
the groupNames of interest to the human genome I had problems of
unknown groupName annotation.

============================
>firma <- FirmaModel(plmTr)
>fit(firma, verbose=verbose)
>fs <- getFirmaScores(firma)
>a <- extractDataFrame(fs, units=NULL, addNames = TRUE) #retrive all data

unitName groupName
ENSG00000170847 U99990105
ENSG00000197167 U98164481
ENSG00000135940 U97628953
ENSG00000187191 4037142
ENSG00000188120 4036737
ENSG00000205944 4031843
ENSG00000129816 4028967
ENSG00000187268 3999985
========================================

In the above the FirmaScores were retrieved using "extractDataFrame",
some unitNames and groupNames were listed from variable "a". Because
the unitName annotations were Ensembl gene names but not Exon IDs. I
tried to map group name to Exons. The annotation file were downloaded
from http://bioinf.wehi.edu.au/folders/mrobinson/exon/human_cdfs/ensembl_cdf_creation/HuEx-1_0-st-v2.probeset.boundaries.csv.
Using this annotation only entries of groupNames such as "4037142"
could be found, but groupNames begining with "U" such as "U99990105"
couldn't be found. Could any one help me find the complete annotation
file for groupNames?

Regards,

Karl

messages.author: 1ff63ac4948de366
messages.subject: Re: [aroma.affymetrix] Unknown groupName using "HuGene-1_0-st-v1_Ensembl47.cdf"
parts:
Hi Karl.

Very good.

OK, so here is the thing. There are two platforms here -- Human Exon
1.0 and Human Gene 1.0. Many of the probes are shared. For example,
~60% of the probes from the Gene 1.0 ST are found on the Exon 1.0
array (this is the case for human and I assume it is similar for mouse/
rat). But, there are also probes on the Gene array that are not found
on bigger Exon array.

One thing to keep in mind ... the group names you see below are there
only because I mapped the genome locations of the probes on the Gene
1.0 array to the probesets (4 probes usually) on the Exon 1.0 array.
That's not to say that all 4 probes from that Exon probeset are
represented on the Gene array though. The group names starting with
'U' represent those probes that are on the Gene but not the Exon
array ... the number after the 'U' is the genome position. So, you
can't expect to find these probes in the Affy's Exon annotation file!

I personally don't think that FIRMA is the way to go on the Gene array
(if you are trying to use the Gene array as an economical exon array
or to get exon-level summaries), simply because for some exons you
have a single probe and others you have 15 ... but I'm interested to
see how you go with it.

I am working on some kind of exon analysis on the Gene arrays, but its
not ready yet.

Hope that helps.
Mark

parts:
Dear Mark,

With your explanation I finally know the reason about the groupNames
beginning with "U". Additionally, it seems that those groupNames not
beginning with "U" such "4037142" are the ones from Human Exon 1.0.

I'm interested in tissue-enriched exons. To find them I simply
calculated the FIRMA scores and get exons with higher scores in
certain tissues using statistical comparison between tissues with the
control of fdr, and fold differences are also calculated. I assumed
the FIRMA score as normalized exon splicing potential. With your
remind of the problems I carefully inspected the algorithm of FIRMA in
your published paper on the journal of Bioinformatics, I think this
strategy may not work the way I thought. I need to pursue other
algorithms to get tissue-enriched exons.

Again, thank you for your kind help and explanation.

Regards,

Karl

messages.subject: Re: [aroma.affymetrix] Re: Unknown groupName using "HuGene-1_0-st-v1_Ensembl47.cdf"
parts:
Hi Karl,

I'm not sure exactly what you mean by "normalized exon splicing
potential", but the FIRMA score should definitely give you an
indication of differential splicing and at least for the Human Exon
1.0 array, should be able to help you find tissue-enriched exons, as
in fact was done in the paper. Nevertheless, I haven't used FIRMA
with the Human Gene 1.0 array, so it's possible (as Mark says) that it
won't work as well in that context.

Incidentally, there was a good discussion on a related topic a couple
of months back. Although it was in the context of exon arrays it may
give you some ideas for analysis strategies. The discussion is
archived here:

http://groups.google.com/group/aroma-affymetrix/browse_thread/thread/7a0f4eb666cab485/e7f16ce24210e9ec?lnk=gst&q=splicing+index#e7f16ce24210e9ec

You could also try searching the group archives for similar discussions.

Cheers,

Ken

messages.subject: Re: Unknown groupName using "HuGene-1_0-st-v1_Ensembl47.cdf"
parts:
Dear Ken,

Thank you very much for your information.

> I'm not sure exactly what you mean by "normalized exon splicing
> potential", but the FIRMA score should definitely give you an
> indication of differential splicing and at least for the Human Exon
> 1.0 array, should be able to help you find tissue-enriched exons, as
> in fact was done in the paper. Nevertheless, I haven't used FIRMA
> with the Human Gene 1.0 array, so it's possible (as Mark says) that it
> won't work as well in that context.

The probe count problem in Human Gene 1.0 array is easy to solve. I
can just filter those with less than 4 probes. And as you said FIRMA
score indeed give an indication of differential splicing. But I can't
tackle my practical problem in finding tissue enriched exons using
FIRMA in an easy automated way. Can we define a single cut-off for
FIRMA score or perform simple t-tests between tissues to get tissue-
enriched exons? I went through your paper, but can't figure out a way.

>
> Incidentally, there was a good discussion on a related topic a couple
> of months back. Although it was in the context of exon arrays it may
> give you some ideas for analysis strategies. The discussion is
> archived here:
>

> http://groups.google.com/group/aroma-affymetrix/browse_thread/thread/...

After going through the previous discussions I think Splicing Index
(SI) may be what I need. Some codes calculate SI were also posted in
the discussion. But the data of exon microarray must come from Cel and
Cdf files. The data I'm very interested in is from GEO (http://
www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/query/acc.cgi?acc=GSE5791), and the probeSet
expression values were already normalized. The probeSet annotation is
outdated. I am now remapping them to the recent Genome Assembly using
Blat. Finally the probeSet can be mapped to the Ensembl Exons using
the new genomic locations.

My question is how can I import these processed data into celsetN
(used in "plmGene <- ExonRmaPlm(celsetN, mergeGroups=TRUE)"). Is there
any technical problem for me to complete the analysis? If it works I
would be very glad if you can refer me some technical references.

The code from previous discusions I wish to use:
===================================================
plmGene <- ExonRmaPlm(celsetN, mergeGroups=TRUE)
fit(plmGene, verbose=verbose)
plmEx <- ExonRmaPlm(celsetN, mergeGroups=FALSE)
fit(plmEx, verbose=verbose)
exDF<-extractDataFrame(plmEx,addNames=TRUE)
exDF[,-c(1:5)]<-log2(exDF[,-c(1:5)]) #the first 5 columns are the
names
geneDF<-extractDataFrame(plmGene,addNames=TRUE)
geneDF[,-c(1:5)]<-log2(geneDF[,-c(1:5)])

calculateSI<-function(geneEffectsDF,exonEffectsDF,skip=1:5){
units<-geneEffectsDF$unitName
if(any(ncol(geneEffectsDF[,-skip])!=ncol(exonEffectsDF[,-skip])))
stop("Matrices do not match")
SIDF<-exonEffectsDF
SIDF[,-skip]<-NA
cumMatch<-NULL
for(i in 1:length(units)){
whMatch<-which(exonEffectsDF$unitName==units[i])
cumMatch<-c(cumMatch,whMatch)
if(length(whMatch)==0){
warning("Unit",i,"is not found in the exon data frame")
next;
}
geneEff<-as.numeric(geneEffectsDF[i,-skip])

SIDF[whMatch,-skip]<-sweep(data.matrix(exonEffectsDF[whMatch,-skip]),
2,geneEff,"-")

}
if(length(cumMatch)!=nrow(exonEffectsDF)) warning("Some units in
exon data frame were not found in the gene data frame")
return(SIDF)
======================================================

Best regards,

Karl

I don't think you'll want to filter probes with less than 4 probes on
the *Gene 1.0* array, as that will leave you with less than 10% of all
exons/probesets in the human genome. Below is a table based on my
calculations of number of probes per probeset for the two chips (rows
- Gene, columns - Exon):

1 2 3 4
1 8,798 3,445 3,521 111,767
2 5 5,485 3,486 102,939
3 0 14 1,735 30,897
4 0 9 21 17,502
>4 0 4 23 7,572

From that link Ken sent, one suggestion was to use something like
limma for determining significant differences in FIRMA score between
tissues. There is your t-test. Cutoffs may work too.

SI may be the way to go, but it suffers the same problem of getting

mention is not Human Gene 1.0 ST data, so maybe I'm misinterpreting
your previous questions regarding the Gene array (or is this a
separate thing?).

As Mark says, it may just be easiest to request the raw probe level
data (and CDFs - assuming you aren't going to create your own based on
your remapping) from Affymetrix, if it isn't already available online
somewhere. A word of warning: the research array came with 4 CDFs, so
there are 4 CEL files for each sample. As I recall the CDF and CEL
files were all in ASCII format, so you may also need to convert them
to binary format in order to (greatly) speed up the analysis. Good
luck with it and let us know if you need more help.

Cheers

Ken

parts:
Dear Ken and Mark,

Thank you for your kind suggestions. And I may indeed need your help
in my work.

I have sent a request for the Cdf files to Affymetrix. In addition, I
am also on the process of remapping probes and reanalyze the whole
available data. However, I found lots of probes not exactly matched to
the recent genome sequence, for the total 1359271 unique probes, only
859919 ones (63.3%) were exactly the same as in the genome. Thus lots
of precious information was lost. I don't know how to deal with the
situation, should I use the best match for those not exactly matched?

Best regards,

Karl

On Thu, Jul 31, 2008 at 11:48 PM, guo <xuejia...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Dear Ken and Mark,
>
> Thank you for your kind suggestions. And I may indeed need your help
> in my work.
>
> I have sent a request for the Cdf files to Affymetrix. In addition, I
> am also on the process of remapping probes and reanalyze the whole
> available data. However, I found lots of probes not exactly matched to
> the recent genome sequence, for the total 1359271 unique probes, only
> 859919 ones (63.3%) were exactly the same as in the genome. Thus lots
> of precious information was lost. I don't know how to deal with the
> situation, should I use the best match for those not exactly matched?

If you are not going to use Affy's annotation, then you won't need
their CDFs, just the CEL files. You will need to create a custom CDF.

I'm surprised that the proportion of probes not exactly matching is so
high. Are you sure that you have _probe_ sequences (25-mers) that you
are matching to the genome sequence? The number of unique probes you
quote appears to match the number of probe _set_ sequences in the GEO
record for the research array. If you want to do the exercise you
describe, you will need to request the probe sequences from Affy, BLAT
them against the genome and then create four different CDFs, because
the research array was actually 4 different arrays (A, B, C, D).

Cheers,

Ken
